The slip frame comprises a center ring and a plurality of slats extending longitudinally uphole and downhole from the center ring and spaced radially about the center ring so as to define at least two pairs of slots. A downhole tool is secured within a wellbore using both a one-way slip and a two-way slip. The two-way slip includes a slip frame together with at least two slip banks. The slip frame includes a central ring and multiple slats that run lengthwise in both the uphole and downhole directions from the central ring. These slats are arranged circumferentially around the central ring to form at least two pairs of slots. In each slot pair, one slot extends lengthwise uphole from the central ring, while the other extends lengthwise downhole from the central ring.

Each slip bank includes a first gripping bank, a second gripping bank, and a groove located between them. Both gripping banks have outer surfaces designed to bite into or hold the casing. The first gripping bank is slidably positioned within the first slot, and the second gripping bank is slidably positioned within the second slot. In a set position, the groove accommodates part of the central ring, while the first and second gripping banks project radially outward from the slip frame so they can contact and grip the casing. In an unset position, the slip bank sits radially inward relative to its set position.

A downhole tool may be secured within a wellbore by using a combination of slip mechanisms, including both a unidirectional slip and a bidirectional slip. The unidirectional slip may be configured to resist movement of the tool in one axial direction, while the bidirectional slip may be configured to resist movement in both uphole and downhole directions. Together, these slips help anchor the downhole tool in place within the casing or wellbore.

The bidirectional slip includes a slip frame and at least two slip banks supported by the slip frame. The slip frame includes a center ring, from which a plurality of longitudinal slats extend in both uphole and downhole directions. The slats are arranged to define paired slots on opposite sides of the center ring. These paired slots provide guide paths or receiving spaces for the slip banks as the bidirectional slip is actuated between unset and set positions.

Each slip bank includes a first gripping bank and a second gripping bank separated by a groove. The first and second gripping banks have outer surfaces configured to engage and grip an inner surface of the casing. For example, the outer surfaces may include teeth, serrations, buttons, hardened inserts, or other gripping features suitable for biting into or frictionally engaging the casing wall.

Each slip bank is movable between an unset position and a set position. In the unset position, the slip bank is positioned radially inward relative to the casing so that the gripping banks do not substantially engage the casing. This allows the downhole tool to be run into the wellbore or moved to a desired location. In the set position, the slip bank is displaced radially outward toward the casing. As the slip bank moves outward, the groove between the first and second gripping banks receives a portion of the center ring of the slip frame. In this set position, the first and second gripping banks engage the casing, thereby anchoring the bidirectional slip and assisting in holding the downhole tool in the wellbore.
outputs.L4:
A downhole wellbore anchoring tool is designed to secure a tool string or other downhole assembly within a casing or wellbore by gripping the surrounding casing wall. The anchoring tool includes a combination of slip assemblies that provide holding capability in both axial directions. In particular, the tool may include a unidirectional slip configured to resist movement in one direction, such as an uphole or downhole direction, and a bidirectional slip configured to resist movement in both directions along the wellbore.

The bidirectional slip includes a slip frame having a plurality of slots or openings formed around its circumference. Within these slots are slideable slip banks that can move radially and/or axially between an unset position and a set position. In the unset position, the slip banks are retracted sufficiently to allow the anchoring tool to be run into or removed from the wellbore without substantially engaging the casing. In the set position, one or more gripping banks are driven outward through the slots in the slip frame so that gripping surfaces, teeth, or inserts on the slip banks contact and bite into the casing wall.

A center ring or central support member may be positioned within or adjacent to the slip frame to help guide and support the slip banks as they move. As the tool is actuated, the slip banks slide relative to the slip frame and the center ring, causing the gripping banks to extend outward around the center ring in a controlled manner. This arrangement allows the slip banks to distribute gripping forces around the circumference of the tool, improving stability and reducing the likelihood of uneven loading or premature release.

When deployed in the wellbore, the unidirectional slip can provide anchoring resistance in one axial direction, while the bidirectional slip provides additional resistance in both the uphole and downhole directions. Together, these slip structures enable the anchoring tool to maintain a secure hold against forces that may act from either direction, such as pressure differentials, tubing movement, operational loads, or forces generated by other downhole tools.

The slideable slip bank configuration also allows the anchoring tool to transition reliably between its unset and set states. During running or retrieval, the slip banks remain retracted to minimize drag and prevent unintended engagement with the casing. During setting, the slip banks move outward into gripping engagement with the casing. Once set, the gripping banks cooperate with the slip frame and center ring to hold the anchoring tool firmly in place within the wellbore.

This construction provides a robust bidirectional anchoring mechanism suitable for use in cased wellbores where secure axial retention is required. By combining unidirectional and bidirectional slip action with a slotted frame and movable slip banks, the tool can grip the casing effectively and resist movement both uphole and downhole, thereby improving the reliability and stability of downhole operations.

**The Power of “The” and “Each”**

The words **“the”** and **“each”** may seem small, but they play an important role in English. **“The”** is used to talk about something specific or already known. For example, when we say, “The book is on the table,” we mean a particular book and a particular table.

**“Each”** is used when we talk about individual members of a group. It helps us focus on every single person or thing separately. For example, “Each student received a certificate” means that every student got one certificate.

Together, these words help make sentences clearer and more precise. **The** points to something specific, while **each** emphasizes individuality. Even though they are short and simple, they are essential for clear communication.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph technical description of a wellbore anchoring device held in casing by a unidirectional slip and a bidirectional slip, emphasizing the structure and set/unset positions of the bidirectional slip assembly.
counterfactuals.output: A wellbore anchoring device is configured to be run into casing on a tubular body and selectively secured against axial movement by a unidirectional slip assembly and a bidirectional slip assembly carried on the body. The unidirectional slip is arranged to bite the casing in response to loading in one axial direction, while the bidirectional slip assembly provides anchoring resistance in both uphole and downhole directions. The bidirectional slip assembly includes a slip carrier or cage disposed around the mandrel, a plurality of circumferentially spaced slip segments mounted in windows or pockets of the carrier, and opposed ramp or cone surfaces positioned to drive the slip segments radially outward when the assembly is actuated. Each slip segment has an outer gripping face with casing-engaging teeth and an inner cam surface cooperating with the opposed cones so that axial compression, tension, or relative movement between the carrier and cones produces radial expansion. In the unset position, the bidirectional slip segments are retained radially inward within or close to the carrier, with the teeth retracted from the casing inner wall to permit running or retrieval of the device through the wellbore. In the set position, relative axial displacement of the bidirectional slip components forces the slip segments outward along the ramp surfaces until the teeth penetrate or frictionally grip the casing, thereby locking the tool against movement in either axial direction. To unset the device, the actuating load is relieved or reversed and the cones are shifted away from the slip segments, allowing springs, retainers, or the natural radial bias of the slip assembly to retract the segments to the unset position and release the casing engagement.

counterfactuals.output:
An invention relates to a downhole tool configured to be retained in a wellbore, such as a cased wellbore, by a bidirectional anchoring assembly. The tool includes a mandrel or tool body and a bidirectional slip assembly disposed about the mandrel. The slip assembly is operable between a run-in position and a set position in which the tool is secured against movement in either axial direction.

The bidirectional slip includes a plurality of circumferentially spaced slip banks. Each slip bank has a first gripping bank and a second gripping bank. The first and second gripping banks may include teeth, wickers, inserts, or other gripping features oriented to resist axial loading in opposite directions along the wellbore. Thus, when the slip is set, one gripping bank resists movement of the tool in an uphole direction while the other gripping bank resists movement in a downhole direction.

A center ring is positioned relative to the slip banks between the first and second gripping banks. Each slip bank includes a groove or recess configured to receive at least a portion of the center ring when the slip assembly is actuated to the set position. As the tool is set, axial compression, cone movement, or another actuator drives the slip banks radially outward into gripping engagement with the surrounding casing or formation. During this movement, the center ring is received in the groove of each slip bank, helping to align, support, or stabilize the slip banks and maintain the bidirectional gripping banks in proper position.

In one implementation, the center ring functions as a spacer, retainer, or guide between oppositely oriented gripping portions of the slip assembly. The engagement between the center ring and the grooves of the slip banks may reduce relative movement, improve load distribution, and inhibit premature separation or misalignment of the gripping banks during setting and loading. The slip assembly therefore provides reliable bidirectional retention of the downhole tool within the wellbore after setting.

counterfactuals.output: A bidirectional slip mechanism for a wellbore tool includes a slip body having uphole and downhole slots configured to receive corresponding sliding gripping banks. The gripping banks are movable relative to the slip body between unset radial positions, in which gripping surfaces are retracted from a surrounding casing, and set radial positions, in which the gripping surfaces extend outward to engage and grip the casing. The uphole and downhole slots orient the gripping banks to resist axial movement of the tool in both uphole and downhole directions when set, while permitting release and radial retraction when unset.
